opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core issue is that "alignment" isn't one thing. When you take a general-purpose model and fine-tune it to be safer or more aligned, you're implicitly choosing a particular set of values and behaviors: what counts as harmful, what counts as fair, what the model should refuse. Those choices are made with some notion of a typical user or a typical use case in mind. But a general-purpose model, by definition, gets deployed in an enormous variety of settings, and the right behavior in one setting can be exactly the wrong behavior in another.

A simple example: suppose you align a model to be very cautious about medical or toxicological information, because you don't want it helping someone do harm. That's quite reasonable for a consumer chatbot. But now imagine a pharmacologist or an emergency room physician using that same model. For them, the cautious behavior is a degradation. The model hedges, refuses, or waters down exactly the information they need. The same thing happens with fairness constraints. In my work on algorithmic fairness, one of the lessons we kept running into is that there are many mathematically distinct definitions of fairness, and they're often mutually incompatible. If you bake one of them into a model, you've made a choice that will look wrong from the perspective of an application that needed a different one.

There's also a more technical point, which is that these are constrained optimization problems. Any time you add a constraint, whether it's a fairness constraint, a privacy constraint, or a behavioral alignment constraint, you're shrinking the set of models you're allowed to choose from. In general that has a cost in raw accuracy or capability somewhere. We've spent a lot of time characterizing those tradeoffs as Pareto frontiers. What's different with foundation models is that you're paying that cost once, upstream, for everybody, even though the benefit of the constraint might only be relevant to some fraction of downstream uses.

So I think the natural conclusion is that we should be more thoughtful about where in the stack alignment happens. Maybe some baseline set of protections belongs in the foundation model. But a lot of the fine-grained, context-dependent alignment probably belongs closer to the application, where you actually know who the user is and what "good behavior" means in that setting. Trying to get one model to be aligned for every possible use at once is, I think, asking for something that's mathematically and practically quite hard.

r001.rationale: The response explains that alignment imposes choices or constraints that can reduce capability and that behavior suited to one setting can impair another, giving medical and fairness examples. This clearly communicates likely performance degradation for some natural use cases.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to say it is that alignment is a form of constraint, and whenever you constrain an optimization problem, you generally give something up. The base model, before any alignment, has essentially been trained to do one thing, which is predict the next token as well as it possibly can across this enormous, heterogeneous distribution of human text. That objective is agnostic. It doesn't care whether the continuation is polite or offensive, helpful or harmful, cautious or confident. It just wants to be right about what comes next.

Then you come along with alignment, whether that's RLHF or some other technique, and you say: actually, there are regions of your behavior that we don't want. Don't produce this kind of content, hedge in these situations, refuse in those. And you're reshaping the model's output distribution to satisfy those preferences. But the preferences you're enforcing are not uniformly compatible with every use case. They were elicited from some population of raters, with some set of guidelines, reflecting some set of values and some notion of what the "typical" user wants. A general-purpose model, by definition, is going to be used by people whose needs are very far from typical.

So take a concrete example. If you're a security researcher or a toxicologist or a novelist writing a villain, the very behaviors that alignment is suppressing may be exactly the ones you need. The model has been trained to be reluctant in precisely your region of the space. And it's not just refusals. I think a subtler cost is what people have started calling the "alignment tax," where the model becomes more verbose, more hedged, more inclined toward a kind of bland consensus answer, because that's what tended to get rewarded. For a lot of tasks, that's fine. For tasks where you want sharp, committed, possibly contrarian output, it's a degradation.

There's also a more technical point, which is that the fine-tuning process itself is relatively low-data compared to pretraining. You're nudging billions of parameters based on a comparatively small number of preference comparisons. It would be surprising if that didn't have side effects beyond the behaviors you were targeting. You wanted the model to refuse to help synthesize dangerous chemicals, and you also, somewhat inadvertently, made it worse at ordinary chemistry. The capabilities aren't cleanly separable inside the network, so when you push on one, others move.

And I'd connect this to work I've done in algorithmic fairness, because it's really the same phenomenon. When you impose a fairness constraint on a classifier, you almost always pay in aggregate accuracy, and the tradeoff curve is often not pretty. Alignment is a fairness-like constraint on a generative model, and I don't think we should be surprised that there's a Pareto frontier here rather than a free lunch. The interesting research question is how to make that frontier as favorable as possible, and whether you can get more customized alignment, where the constraints reflect the actual deployment context rather than a one-size-fits-all compromise.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment constrains the model and generally entails giving something up, then explains that its preferences can conflict with some users’ needs and degrade performance on those use cases.

astra-6.text:
Well, a general-purpose language model is going to be used by many different people for many different purposes. And those people won’t necessarily agree on what constitutes desirable behavior. The same response might be exactly what one user wants and something another user finds inappropriate or unhelpful. So alignment isn’t just turning a knob that makes the model universally better. You’re choosing which behaviors to encourage and which to discourage.

For example, you might train a model to be cautious about providing potentially harmful information. That can be valuable, but it can also cause it to decline a legitimate question from someone studying that topic. You’ve improved one aspect of its behavior while making it less useful for that particular task.

So I think the important question is: aligned with whose preferences, and for what use? With a general-purpose model, there’s no reason to expect that a single answer to that question will improve performance for everyone.

r001.rationale: The response explains that alignment favors some behaviors over others and can make a legitimate use less useful, then says a single alignment choice should not be expected to improve performance for everyone.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, alignment isn’t a single objective that everybody agrees on. You’re taking a general-purpose model and adjusting its behavior toward some set of preferences—what it should say, what it should refuse, how cautious it should be. And those preferences may make it less useful for a particular user or task.

For example, you might want a model to avoid providing dangerous instructions. But the same knowledge could be useful to somebody doing legitimate security research. If the model can’t reliably distinguish those contexts, making it safer can also cause it to refuse useful requests.

So I think the important question is: aligned with whom, and for what purpose? We shouldn’t assume there’s one adjustment that makes a model better along every dimension for every application. There are trade-offs, and we need to evaluate those trade-offs in the context where the model will actually be used.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment preferences may make a model less useful for particular tasks and describes trade-offs, but it does not state that degradation for some natural use cases is almost inevitable.
